title: Geopolitical coexistence judgments combine shared distrust with different attributed obstacles
source_unit: Pew Research Center Spring 2026 Global Attitudes Survey; Israeli adults and Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem
geography: Israel and West Bank/East Jerusalem; Gaza not surveyed

observations.period: Israeli fieldwork April 5-May 6, 2026; West Bank/East Jerusalem fieldwork March 30-April 28, 2026; report September 15, 2026

denominator.unit: Israeli adults surveyed; separate West Bank/East Jerusalem sample n=1038

coexistence_possible_israel.unit: percent of Israeli adults saying Israel and an independent Palestinian state could coexist peacefully

coexistence_possible_west_bank_east_jeru.unit: percent of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem saying coexistence could be peaceful

coexistence_not_possible.unit: percent saying peaceful coexistence is not possible

attributed_obstacles.value: Open-ended explanations include land and identity conflict, historical and recent violence, distrust, perceived existential threat among Israelis, and occupation/control, checkpoints, and lack of security or political rights among Palestinians
attributed_obstacles.unit: coded themes in respondents' own explanations

observations.method: Face-to-face survey under Gallup direction in Hebrew and Arabic, followed by an open-ended request for respondents to explain their coexistence judgment; Pew coded the explanations into recurring themes.
observations.uncertainty: Fieldwork occurred during the Iran war and around an initial ceasefire. Gaza was not surveyed. Open-ended coding captures stated explanations, not a causal test of why attitudes formed or whether they predict behavior.
observations.subgroup: Israeli adults, including Jewish and Arab Israelis, and Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem; Pew also reports differences by political coalition support and ethnicity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Pessimism may reflect wartime salience and immediate security conditions rather than a permanent cultural disposition. Shared categories such as distrust do not imply that the two populations attribute responsibility, risk, or a feasible remedy in the same way.

related_sources.claim: Pew's open-ended response coding methodology and sample details.

boundary: This record adds a geopolitical meaning and attribution layer. It does not establish a causal effect of war, occupation, leadership, aid, or identity on attitudes, and it does not measure later political action, reconciliation, or counterpart behavior.
